articles.title: US offers $20 million reward for information on Iran's nuclear programme
articles.summary: The United States is offering a reward of up to $20 million, along with possible relocation, for information about Iran's nuclear programme, including its
articles.body: The United States is offering a reward of up to $20 million, along with possible relocation, for information about Iran's nuclear programme, including its facilities, equipment and personnel, as diplomatic efforts continue to secure a deal to end the more than eight-month-old war.US Central Command (Centcom) announced the offer on Friday through a post on X, saying the State Department's Rewards for Justice programme was seeking information about Iran's nuclear activities, including details about scientists and the movement of related equipment and personnel."Rewards for Justice is offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above," Centcom said.The programme was established in 1984 under the State Department's national security rewards initiative to offer financial incentives for information that protects American lives and interests.In its statement, the State Department said Iran's "lack of compliance with the IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency) on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like centrifuges".It did not specify what information would qualify for the maximum $20 million reward.Trump says Iran wants deal as diplomatic efforts continueThe announcement came as US President Donald Trump reiterated that Tehran was keen to reach an agreement to end the conflict, while claiming that Iran's economy and military had been severely damaged over eight months of war."We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," Trump said on Friday night in West Palm Beach, Florida.He also defended the US military campaign against Iran, saying, "If we didn't hit Iran, you wouldn't have Israel today. If they had nuclear, they would have used nuclear. They would have obliterated the Middle East."Trump has repeatedly claimed that US forces have effectively obliterated Iran's nuclear programme. Earlier this week, he said he still had to "take care" of one or two targets, including the so-called Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site that Tehran denies is a nuclear facility.Diplomatic efforts by mediators have continued to prevent a resumption of fighting. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said earlier this week that his government was still trying to resolve the crisis through dialogue.US carries out fresh strikes as Qatar pushes proposalsMeanwhile, Trump said the US military carried out fresh, limited strikes on Iran on Friday, targeting its air defence systems. He described the action as "minor", saying the military had knocked out an Iranian anti-aircraft device within minutes.Iranian state media reported hearing two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which lies in the Strait of Hormuz. Friday's strikes were the first since Trump's Republican Party suffered a setback in Tuesday's US midterm elections, losing both chambers of Congress.Earlier on Friday, two Middle East government officials told news agency AP that Iran was reviewing proposals presented by Qatar, the chief mediator, to address differences with Washington over Tehran's nuclear programme.The officials said Iran was, however, unwilling to enter negotiations on its nuclear activities until the US agreed to several conditions demanded by Tehran as part of a ceasefire agreement.The reported proposals include a two-day set of trust-building measures. These involve lifting the US blockade on Iran's ports and releasing some of Tehran's frozen funds in exchange for allowing International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to visit sites bombed by the US and Israel, according to regional officials cited by AP.On the second day, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz under a modified arrangement reached with Oman but not approved by the US, the officials said.This would be a temporary measure until a permanent agreement on the waterway could be reached with other Gulf countries.The US and Iran would then begin broader negotiations covering Tehran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium and other aspects of its nuclear programme, according to the officials.Iran has maintained that its nuclear programme is peaceful. The International Atomic Energy Agency has said the country has 440.9 kg of uranium enriched to 60 per cent purity, a short technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90 per cent, AP reported.Iran has also demanded an end to the US blockade, the lifting of sanctions, the unfreezing of its assets, compensation for war damage and an end to hostilities across the region, including Israeli operations in Lebanon, before entering nuclear talks.Diplomatic contacts have intensified in recent days. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth spoke to his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, on Friday about developments in the region. Trump also spoke to Qatar's emir about efforts to de-escalate tensions.Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi held separate calls with his Iraqi and Tunisian counterparts.During his conversation with Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein, Araghchi discussed Tehran's position on resuming negotiations with Washington, according to Iraq's News Agency.Egyptian foreign minister Badr Abdelatty also called for flexibility from both sides to reach compromise solutions and prevent another escalation in the region.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Trinamool Congress (TMC) National General Secretary Abhishek Banerjee on Saturday alleged that his residence was attacked by Bharatiya Janata
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Trinamool Congress (TMC) National General Secretary Abhishek Banerjee on Saturday alleged that his residence was attacked by Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) workers around 2 am, accusing the Kolkata Police of failing to prevent the incident.He also claimed that it was the seventh attempt on his life in the past six months and accused the judiciary of turning a blind eye to the alleged attacks.The BJP hit back at Banerjee over his allegations, with West Bengal Minister Dilip Ghosh dismissing them as an attempt to mislead people. Questioning who would want to kill the TMC leader, Ghosh said, "This is the first time we’ve seen a politician’s birthday being celebrated on the footpath. If someone creates a disturbance, there is bound to be a backlash. Besides, who has the time to kill Abhishek Banerjee? There is nothing left for them to say or do, so they are attempting to mislead people by bringing up this issue."In a post on social media platform X, Banerjee alleged that the attack took place shortly after he released a video showing unidentified individuals conducting reconnaissance of his office and residence."After I released the recce video this morning, my house was attacked just now, at 2 AM by BJP goons, right under the watch of the Kolkata police," he said.The TMC leader also criticised the Calcutta High Court and the Supreme Court over their alleged inaction, saying, "Thank you, Calcutta High Court and the Supreme Court of India, for remaining mute spectators while all this unfolds. I will upload the videos shortly."In a subsequent post, Banerjee shared footage of the alleged attack and accused BJP workers of targeting his residence after conducting reconnaissance for two days. He also alleged that neither the police nor the judiciary had taken action despite repeated threats to his life."After two days of continuous recce, this is how BJP hooligans attacked my house at 2 AM today. Watch the footage and see for yourself. If this is what can happen to an elected Member of Parliament, imagine the plight of the common man in WB.This is the seventh attempt on my life in the last six months. Yet, there has been no police action and no judicial intervention. Hooligans are running riot across the state because the judiciary continues to turn a blind eye.Thank you, Milords, for remaining mute spectators!" he said.The allegations followed Banerjee's claims on Friday that unidentified individuals had been monitoring his office and residence for the past two days. He alleged that the individuals identified themselves as police personnel when confronted."For the past two days, a few unidentified individuals have been conducting reconnaissance of my office and residence. The registration number of their motorcycle is mentioned below. When confronted, they claimed to be police personnel," he said.Questioning the alleged surveillance, Banerjee asked who had authorised the state police to monitor the premises of an elected Member of Parliament and for what purpose."Why is the State Police allegedly spying on and snooping around the office and residence of an elected Member of Parliament? Who authorised this surveillance and for what purpose?" he asked.Describing the alleged surveillance as a suspected conspiracy, Banerjee called for an immediate and thorough investigation and urged the Lok Sabha Speaker, Kolkata Police, Union Home Ministry and West Bengal Police to identify those involved and establish who had ordered the operation."I am immediately drawing the attention of the Hon’ble Speaker of the Lok Sabha @ombirlakota, @kolkata_police, @HMOIndia @WBPolice to this extremely serious matter. I demand an immediate and thorough inquiry to establish the identity of these individuals, who sent them and to uncover the nefarious motive behind this suspected conspiracy," he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Grow veggies in your front lawn
articles.summary: Can cities grow some of the food they consume? Turf grass is US’s third largest crop after corn and soy.
articles.body: Can cities grow some of the food they consume?Turf grass is US’s third largest crop after corn and soy. In Tiny Gardens Everywhere: A History of Urban Resilience, Kate Brown asks, why would 135mn homeowners and renters in US, who keep lawns, make the effort, and foot the expense, to maintain a crop, they can neither eat, nor sell. The tale she goes on to tell is that of the tangled garden of inequality, and an equal resistance, born of hardship and ecological wisdom. Picks from the garden:l In England, the 1800s’ takeover of commons by elites, municipalities, developers resulted in territories divided, protected, guarded. Tradition of people farming common land was upended in the land grab. Brown says this was also a way of controlling labour. Privatising commons left workers with no choice but to sell their labour in factories. Widespread worker unrest led to attacks on property and authorities. To calm tensions, small parcels of land were allotted to grow vegetable gardens. The plots had degraded soil. But still, those who tried it saved around 20% of household expenses, encouraging others to join.Their success made these a symbol of private property, social hierarchy. Who’d get one depended on family history, criminal record, employment, church attendance etc. Men who joined labour unions didn’t get plots. Nor did women. “Compared to common rights, allotments were a symbol of dispossession.” But still, these helped striking worker families tide over hard times.l With rapid urbanisation, grass lawns replaced gardens. Turf grass – from France to England to US – became a marker of respectability, a middle-class symbol, of property value and order. Rules criminalised front yard plants taller than 6 to 8 inches. In Montgomery (US), Georgette Norman’s garden out front became an act of resistance against restrictions on growing food in front yards. Official crackdown destroyed her garden, made her out to be a criminal, but she neither gave up, nor gave in. A new mayor annulled all cases against her. Her garden survived.l Hunger during war – butter riots 1915, potato riots 1916, bread riots 1917 – radicalised German politics. Brown says, “Gnawing stomachs…elevated tiny allotment gardens to national importance.” Architects, urban planners, and politicians embraced tiny gardens as the solution to wartime scarcity. With a rally cry of ‘Every Working Man A Garden’, post-war Germany moved swiftly to legislate the Small Gardens Act (July 1919).l Industrial agriculture’s failings, climate challenges and soil degradation globally, have led to a realisation that development czars and aid agencies have exported failing farming systems to people who had healthy, diverse community of crops.In Amsterdam, resistance against building a warehouse took the form of a proposal to build a food park. A kitchen garden taken to scale. The plan included “community gardens, urban farms…making healthy food more affordable.” From the food park, densely urbanised Netherlands took another leap, creating food forests, a layered urban forest with the fruit and nut trees, herbs and veggies, climbers and edible roots/tubers. Can growing food in gardens restore biodiversity? They certainly have a better shot at it than sprawling lawns.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: From mass deportations to White House chief, how Stephen Miller became Trump's key pick
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has appointed longtime adviser Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, placing one of the architects of his
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has appointed longtime adviser Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, placing one of the architects of his hardline immigration agenda at the centre of his administration as he prepares for an expected political confrontation with Democrats following the Republican Party's losses in the midterm elections.Trump announced the staffing change on Friday, describing Miller as one of his "most trusted" advisers. Miller, 41, will take over the role on Monday, replacing Susie Wiles, who has served as chief of staff throughout Trump's second term.The appointment comes as Democrats prepare to launch sweeping investigations into the administration, including its immigration enforcement policies. With Democrats gaining control of Congress, Miller is expected to play a key role in defending the president's agenda and managing the administration's response to congressional scrutiny.Miller's elevation is also being viewed as a sign that Trump intends to maintain his America First agenda rather than retreat from some of his most controversial policies following the electoral setback."The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic," Miller said on Friday.Why Trump chose Stephen MillerMiller has been among Trump's closest advisers and has played a central role in shaping immigration policy during both of his administrations. His appointment places an experienced policy strategist and a strong advocate of the president's immigration agenda in a key position as the White House prepares for battles with a Democrat-controlled Congress.Also read: Stephen Miller - Key architect of Trump's immigration crackdown appointed White House chief of staffDuring Trump's second term, Miller has held a broad policy portfolio but has remained particularly influential in driving the administration's efforts to accelerate deportations of undocumented immigrants, a central promise of Trump's 2024 presidential campaign.He also pushed for an expansion of immigration enforcement, including urging Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to make at least 3,000 arrests a day. In May 2025, he publicly called for a sharp increase in daily arrests, putting pressure on the agency's leadership and widening enforcement beyond immigrants convicted of serious crimes.Miller also proposed deploying the National Guard to support mass deportations and backed the administration's expansion of third-country deportations, under which immigrants were sent to countries where they had neither citizenship nor family ties, including several African nations.His enforcement agenda was supported by approximately $170 billion allocated by congressional Republicans for immigration enforcement and border security under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which became law in July 2025.Miller's role in Trump's controversial immigration policiesMiller's influence on Trump's immigration agenda dates back to the president's first term. He helped develop and publicly defend the executive order restricting entry into the United States by nationals of several Muslim-majority countries. The travel ban triggered protests and legal challenges, with its third iteration upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.He was also a leading advocate of the administration's 2018 zero-tolerance policy for illegal border crossings, which resulted in thousands of children being separated from their families. Trump eventually backed away from the policy.Miller also pushed for reductions in refugee admissions. The administration repeatedly lowered the annual ceiling, setting it at 15,000 for the 2021 fiscal year, then a record low.His policy priorities extended to legal immigration as well. Miller advocated penalising legal immigrants who received public benefits and making it more difficult for them to obtain US citizenship.During Trump's second term, he supported the use of the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 to expedite the deportation of alleged Venezuelan gang members to El Salvador, where they were held at the CECOT maximum-security prison. The move triggered a legal battle, and the Supreme Court blocked the administration from immediately deporting Venezuelans without giving them an opportunity to challenge their removal.In May 2025, Miller also said the administration was considering suspending the constitutional mechanism that allows detainees to challenge their confinement in court.At a conference in Miami in March 2026, he argued that military force, rather than conventional criminal law enforcement alone, was necessary to defeat drug cartels.Also read: Trump appoints Stephen Miller as chief of staff after GOP’s midterm defeat, sacks Susie WilesHe also appeared alongside Trump in the Oval Office this summer when the president signed executive orders seeking to deny citizenship to certain children born in the United States, after the Supreme Court struck down an earlier order seeking to end birthright citizenship.Political challenges behind the appointmentMiller's appointment comes at a time when Trump's immigration agenda is facing growing political scrutiny. Although polls in 2024 showed that most Hispanic voters supported mass deportations in principle and backed Trump in large numbers, reports of individual cases of immigration enforcement prompted a backlash within the community.Republicans lost Hispanic support in the midterm elections, undermining expectations of a lasting political realignment in the party's favour. The electoral setback has added to the pressure on the administration as Democrats prepare to scrutinise its immigration policies.Trump has previously retreated from some of the hardline measures championed by Miller. During his first term in 2018, the president imposed the Miller-backed zero-tolerance policy that led to family separations at the US-Mexico border, but subsequently backed away from it.Miller's appointment therefore signals Trump's decision to place a close and influential adviser, who has consistently pushed for tougher immigration enforcement, in a central leadership role as the administration faces mounting political and congressional challenges.You use AI every day. articles.body: BENGALURU: Police have recovered the bodies of Sunitha, wife of accused S Indushekhar, and her mother Rupavathi from a forest area in Salem district of Tamil Nadu, taking the number of bodies recovered in the Bengaluru serial murder case to three.A 12-member team comprising family members has left for Salem to identify the bodies and complete the necessary legal formalities, police said.Investigators have also found that Indushekhar allegedly removed gold ornaments from the bodies of his wife and three other women before disposing of them. He is suspected to have sold some of the jewellery, and police are now tracing the transactions as part of the investigation.According to his alleged confession, Indushekhar killed Sunitha on the night of October 14. The following day, his daughter called Rupavathi and invited her home for dinner, telling her that they would have mutton curry. Indushekhar allegedly told police that he sedated the victims with sleeping pills and bludgeoned them after they fell asleep.Police also recovered at least half a dozen perfume bottles from his Toyota Etios (KA-02-AF-1488), which is being examined as part of the investigation.The postmortem report of seven-year-old victim Puneeth, who was allegedly killed on October 29, confirmed four blunt-force injuries to his head, including the forehead and crown, investigators said.The 52-year-old cab driver was arrested near Ulsoorgate in Bengaluru on Wednesday. Police suspect he killed his wife and six members of her extended family over a 15-day period in October. The murders allegedly took place at his rented house in Rajajinagar between October 16 and 31. He is accused of crushing the victims with a grindstone before wrapping their bodies in multiple layers of plastic covers and placing them in gunny bags.Investigators suspect the killings stemmed from a prolonged marital dispute and resentment towards his wife's relatives, whom he blamed for supporting her during their conflicts.His 17-year-old daughter is suspected to have assisted him in some of the murders and in disposing of the bodies. A 10-year-old boy, the son of two victims, was found in the accused's car when police arrested him. articles.title: 'Gave her everything but weapon’: Man sues OpenAI, claims ChatGPT aided wife in murder plot
articles.summary: A lawsuit filed by a North Carolina man alleges that OpenAI’s ChatGPT provided personalised guidance to his wife on how to poison him, allegedly helping
articles.body: A lawsuit filed by a North Carolina man alleges that OpenAI’s ChatGPT provided personalised guidance to his wife on how to poison him, allegedly helping her plan an attempt on his life. James Gates claims chatbot conversations played a role in the alleged plot by his wife, Cheryl Harris Gates, who was charged with attempted murder after investigators uncovered evidence linked to the case.The allegations came to light during Gates’ appearance on Elizabeth Vargas Reports, where he described how a handwritten note left by his wife led to a police investigation and eventually exposed what he believes was an alleged poisoning attempt.According to a report by News Nation, Gates said he had suffered months of unexplained symptoms, including blackouts, shaking and pain. He initially suspected an illness such as Covid-19 or the flu.The turning point came when he discovered a handwritten note his wife had left on a legal pad. He said it referred to medications, including a generic form of Klonopin, a prescription benzodiazepine and central nervous system depressant, as well as oleander.The note also carried the instruction: “Clear all convos – log out of ChatGPT.”Gates handed the note to police, triggering an investigation into the alleged poisoning.“When I read the note, all of the strange things came into focus. It was obviously the most surreal moment of my life,” Gates said.“I felt like I was in an episode of a true crime that you see on TV,” he added. “She was held in jail for six months. I had no clue at the time why she would do this.”Lawsuit alleges chatbot gave personalised poisoning guidanceAccording to Gates, investigators subsequently uncovered extensive evidence and charged his wife with attempted murder. However, he said he struggled for months to understand what could have motivated the alleged plot.“I would have never thought this would happen … I was perplexed,” Gates said. “It took me months until I had a semblance of what was going on.”Detectives obtained search warrants for his wife's chatbot conversations. However, Gates said investigators initially refused to let him examine the records because the investigation was ongoing.He said he finally gained access to the transcripts in January 2026 after reading an article about teenagers allegedly using chatbots to inflict self-harm.“It wasn’t until January 2026 I saw an article about teens inflicting self-harm using chatbots,” Gates said. “The more I read the transcripts, the more it sounded like my wife.”Meetali Jain, the lawyer representing Gates, said the lawsuit accuses OpenAI of producing a defective product and violating consumer protection laws.Jain alleged that ChatGPT encouraged harmful behaviour and provided information that supported the alleged poisoning plan.“This information was tailored specifically to how Cheryl could poison James, and that information was very personalized…it gave her everything but the weapon,” she said.Case adds to growing scrutiny of AI safetyThe lawsuit comes amid growing scrutiny of artificial intelligence companies and questions over their responsibility when users allegedly act on harmful advice generated by chatbots.OpenAI has not publicly responded to the allegations discussed during the interview.NewsNation has previously reported on other alleged poisoning attempts involving spouses. These include a California dermatologist accused of putting drain cleaner in her husband's tea and an Arizona woman accused of spiking her husband's coffee with bleach.In both cases, investigators said the alleged victims became suspicious after experiencing unexplained illnesses and collecting evidence themselves.You use AI every day. articles.title: Republicans spent more, Democrats won more: Inside the costliest US midterm battle
articles.summary: The 2026 US midterm elections saw record campaign spending, with Republicans spending a whopping 60% more than Democrats but still lost seven stronghold
articles.body: The 2026 US midterm elections saw record campaign spending, with Republicans spending a whopping 60% more than Democrats but still lost seven stronghold seats.The results also reflected growing opposition to data centre projects and a shift in Latino voters' support towards Democrats. The party won both chambers of Congress despite Republicans spending significantly more on Senate races.The elections also showed a change in voting patterns across several states, with many Latino voters moving back towards Democrats after backing Republicans in recent elections.The 2026 midterm elections are expected to be the most expensive in US history, according to nonpartisan watchdog group OpenSecrets. Outside groups and independent committees spent at least $2 billion on the US Senate races, Reuters reported.This was separate from the money spent directly by candidates.Texas was among the biggest spending battlegrounds. Elon Musk, the world's richest person, and other wealthy Republicans spent $316 million to support state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who struggled to raise money for his campaign.Democratic groups spent $109 million backing James Talarico, whose campaign raised more than $146 million directly.Ohio and Michigan also saw spending run into hundreds of millions of dollars, with the amount sewlling more as the Election Day approached.Political groups also changed where they spent their money as the chances of candidates shifted.Spending in Georgia and North Carolina fell as Republican candidates lost ground. At the same time, more money went into South Carolina, Mississippi and Kansas as competitive races emerged in states that were earlier considered safe for Republicans.Outside groups were able to move their spending quickly between states as the election picture changed.Voters push back against data centre projectsOpposition to data centre projects also gained support during the elections. Voters across 10 states backed restrictions on data centre development or rejected plans to build such facilities in their neighbourhoods.According to tracking by Redbud Consulting, 40 of the 41 ballot measures restricted the setting up of data centres.In most counties where these measures were put to a vote, voters also shifted strongly towards Democrats.The election results were followed by a fall in shares of companies linked to artificial intelligence and data centres. These stocks declined in the days after the polls amid expectations of tighter oversight under a Democrat-led US Congress.Record number of Latino voters shift towards DemocratsA major change in the elections came from Latino voters, many of whom moved back towards Democrats after helping Republicans gain ground in recent elections.The shift was seen across different parts of the country, from Texas border counties and meatpacking towns in southwest Kansas to Miami-Dade, Colorado and Arizona.A record number of Latinos voted in the elections, with the figure reaching as many as 14.5 million, said Janet Murguía, CEO of UnidosUS, the largest US Latino civil rights organisation.“Latino voters sent a clear message about their anger and concern about the direction of our country,” she said.The change in Latino voting patterns was part of a larger shift among voters from different racial backgrounds. This broader coalition helped Democrats return to power and win both chambers of Congress, with victories across the country.Republicans lose support in majority-Latino countiesThe shift towards Democrats was also clear in voting data from counties with large Latino populations.Across 64 majority-Latino counties with Senate races where most votes had been counted, Republicans lost 14 percentage points from their 2024 vote share, according to Reuters. This drop was larger than the national trend.In Hidalgo County, Texas, Republican support fell by around 25 percentage points. In Miami-Dade, Florida, a county Trump won in 2024, it dropped by 10 percentage points.These figures show the scale of the shift in Latino voting patterns across key parts of the country.You use AI every day. articles.title: Iran rebuilding missile sites, moving military infrastructure underground to evade strikes
articles.summary: Iran is rapidly rebuilding its military infrastructure damaged by months of US and Israeli airstrikes, with new satellite images showing construction and
articles.body: Iran is rapidly rebuilding its military infrastructure damaged by months of US and Israeli airstrikes, with new satellite images showing construction and excavation work at several key missile bases, according to a report by the New York Post citing BBC Verify. The developments come amid renewed military tensions, with US President Donald Trump confirming fresh limited strikes on an Iranian air defence system.Satellite images taken in November show signs of construction and digging at two major Iranian military installations: the Garmdareh base in Karaj, near Tehran, and the Shahroud base in northern Iran. Analysts from British intelligence company MAIAR, who examined the images, told BBC Verify that at least 12 other military sites, including missile complexes and airbases, also showed signs of repairs and reconstruction.The images reportedly show significant excavation work at both bases, along with vehicles and improvements at the Karaj facility. Former CIA analyst and Iran expert Jim Lamson told BBC Verify that the digging near Shahroud could be linked to missile production. He suggested that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps may be attempting to relocate production facilities underground after repeated airstrikes on a nearby airbase.An MAIAR analyst told the outlet that Iran had demonstrated “a pattern of moving infrastructure underground to protect them from further strikes”. Defence analyst and former head of the Irish military Mark Mellett said underground facilities could make it harder for adversaries to establish the full extent of Iran's military capabilities.The rebuilding efforts come even as Washington continues to target Iranian military assets. Trump said on Friday that the US military had carried out limited strikes against an Iranian air defence system on Qeshm Island, describing the operation as “minor". “They knocked out -- they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five," he said.The strikes followed earlier US attacks on Iranian targets this week. US officials have previously assessed that Tehran would attempt to restore its air defence systems and other military infrastructure after much of its capabilities were destroyed or severely weakened during the June 2025 bombardment by Israel and the early stages of the current conflict.Meanwhile, diplomatic efforts to prevent further escalation are gathering pace, with Qatar presenting proposals aimed at bringing Washington and Tehran back to negotiations over Iran's nuclear programme. However, Tehran has demanded several concessions, including an end to the US blockade, sanctions relief and compensation for war damage, before agreeing to talks.You use AI every day. articles.title: Cha Eunwoo donated 10 million won to a South Korean ALS charity campaign in 2023; two years later, a 23.9 billion won hospital with 76 beds opened after a collective fundraising effort backed by 350,000 donors
articles.summary: South Korean actor and singer Cha Eunwoo's contribution to an ALS awareness campaign in 2023 was among the many efforts supporting patients living with
articles.body: South Korean actor and singer Cha Eunwoo's contribution to an ALS awareness campaign in 2023 was among the many efforts supporting patients living with the progressive neurological disease. Two years later, the fundraising mission reached a significant milestone with the opening of the Seungil Hope Nursing Hospital in Yongin, Gyeonggi Province. Reports by Star Today, The Korea JoongAng Daily, The Korea Times and South Korea's Yonhap News Agency document the journey from celebrity contributions and public donations to the completion of the specialised facility. In July 2023, Cha participated in the 2023 Ice Bucket Challenge after being nominated by actor Lee Jung-jae. Rather than taking part by pouring ice water over himself, the ASTRO member chose to contribute financially, donating 10 million won to support people living with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), commonly known as Lou Gehrig's disease. According to Star Today, Cha also encouraged greater public attention towards people affected by rare and incurable illnesses and their families. He nominated fellow ASTRO member Yoon San-ha and actors Moon Ga-young and Park Gyu-young to continue the campaign. The initiative was part of a wider fundraising movement associated with the Seungil Hope Foundation, which had been working towards establishing a specialised hospital for ALS patients.A 14-year effort finally reaches its goalThe hospital's origins go back to 2011, when former professional basketball coach Park Seung-il and singer Sean established the Seungil Hope Foundation. Park had been diagnosed with ALS at the age of 31 and subsequently dedicated much of his life to raising awareness about the condition and securing better care for patients.Sean, who remained closely involved in the project, helped lead fundraising activities over the years, including the revival of the Ice Bucket Challenge in South Korea. According to The Korea Times, more than 350,000 individual donors contributed towards the hospital's construction, which required an investment of nearly 24 billion won. The project also received support from corporate partners and government funding. Park, however, did not live to see the facility completed. He died in September 2024, around six months before its official opening.What the new hospital offers patientsOn March 31, 2025, the Seungil Hope Nursing Hospital officially opened in Yongin, becoming South Korea's first specialised nursing hospital dedicated to patients with ALS and other severe neuromuscular disorders. The facility was constructed with a total investment of 23.9 billion won, including approximately 12 billion won in government funding and 11.9 billion won raised through donations. The fundraising effort brought together around 350,000 contributors.Spanning approximately 5,000 square metres, the hospital has two basement levels, four floors above ground and 76 beds. It also includes rehabilitation facilities, family visitation areas and spaces for cultural and recreational activities. As reported by Yonhap News Agency, the facility is designed to provide specialised medical care and support for people with severe muscular conditions.ALS gradually affects the nerve cells responsible for controlling voluntary muscle movements. As the disease progresses, patients can lose their ability to walk, speak, swallow and breathe independently. Many require ventilators, feeding tubes and continuous medical assistance. The hospital aims to address these complex needs through round-the-clock care, specialised caregiving services and rehabilitation support, while also easing the considerable responsibilities placed on patients' families.The opening ceremony brought together more than 200 people, including donors, healthcare professionals, public officials and several celebrities who had supported the foundation's work. The completion of the hospital marked a significant moment for the foundation and the families it hopes to serve. What began as a personal mission by a former basketball coach eventually became a collective effort involving hundreds of thousands of people, with the new facility offering specialised care to a community that has long faced limited treatment and caregiving options.You use AI every day. articles.title: US intelligence believes Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had romantic ties with Chinese spy : Report
articles.summary: The US government believes Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman suspected of spying for Beijing, according
articles.body: The US government believes Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman suspected of spying for Beijing, according to a US intelligence memo cited by the Financial Times (FT).The memo, prepared earlier this year using information gathered by American intelligence agencies, alleged that Huang was romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed. US intelligence believes she was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, the country's main intelligence agency, sources told FT.The findings were reportedly circulated among a small group of senior US government officials shortly before President Donald Trump travelled to Beijing for a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.The allegations come amid growing scrutiny of Megaspeed over concerns that advanced Nvidia chips may have been diverted to China in violation of US export controls. The company, which was spun off from a Chinese gaming firm in 2023, buys chips to build data centres and rents computing capacity to customers, including those in China.What is the alleged China spy link?The intelligence findings follow a New York Times report that US officials had identified Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, as a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The report said surveillance had revealed her close relationship with Jensen Huang and that she was allegedly passing information to Beijing.The developments have raised national security concerns in Washington, particularly over the possibility that someone with access to Nvidia's chief executive could have provided sensitive information to China amid intensifying competition between the two countries in artificial intelligence.US officials have also been investigating companies in Southeast Asia suspected of helping divert advanced American chips to China. Washington has sought to restrict Beijing's access to high-performance semiconductors that could strengthen its AI capabilities and military modernisation.The allegations also put a spotlight on Huang's engagement with the Trump administration. The Nvidia chief has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on chip exports to China, arguing that American companies should be allowed to compete in the Chinese market.Earlier this year, Huang personally pushed for permission to sell Nvidia's H200 chips to Chinese customers. Trump subsequently allowed certain chip exports under an arrangement that included a 25 per cent payment to the US government.Huang has also held several meetings with Trump since the president began his second term in 2025. According to FT, he was not initially included among the business leaders accompanying Trump on Air Force One for his May visit to China. After learning of the omission, Trump reportedly called Huang, who later joined the presidential delegation during a stopover in Alaska.Huang also attended a state dinner hosted by Trump for Xi during the Chinese president's September visit to the US.How has Nvidia responded?Nvidia declined to comment on the intelligence memo or the allegations of a romantic relationship between its chief executive and Alice Huang, FT reported. The company has previously maintained that Huang meets thousands of customer executives every year.Responding to the earlier New York Times report, Nvidia said it had already debunked claims that Megaspeed was involved in smuggling its chips into China. Company spokesman John Rizzo said customers such as Megaspeed received ordinary business information rather than sensitive trade secrets or information relevant to national security.Megaspeed had earlier said its current leadership took the allegations seriously and was committed to establishing the facts. China's embassy had dismissed the accusations as groundless smears against the country.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A chef’s Facebook post seeking volunteers and a kitchen led to 5,000 daily meals at Wembley Stadium and more than 4.5 million free meals for Londoners
articles.summary: A chef’s Facebook post asking for volunteers and a kitchen helped launch a food project that went on to prepare more than 5,000 meals a day at Wembley
articles.body: A chef’s Facebook post asking for volunteers and a kitchen helped launch a food project that went on to prepare more than 5,000 meals a day at Wembley Stadium during the COVID-19 pandemic. Leon Aarts posted the request days before the UK lockdown, hoping to use surplus food to make 1,000 meals a day for Londoners. The response grew quickly, and about six weeks later, the team was cooking at Wembley.According to Prism the Gift Fund (2025), the project has provided more than 4.5 million free meals to Londoners since 2020. The work involved hundreds of volunteers, chefs and drivers, as well as daily cooking and deliveries.How did the chef turn surplus food into thousands of mealsAarts was originally a fine dining chef and restaurateur. Before the UK lockdown, he was concerned that people could go hungry as jobs were lost and household finances came under pressure. He posted on Facebook asking who would help him use surplus food to cook meals for Londoners. He had set an initial target of 1,000 meals each day.The appeal attracted a rapid response, with people volunteering their time and skills. The project expanded quickly, and six weeks after the post, the team was preparing more than 5,000 meals a day from Wembley Stadium. The effort brought together volunteers, chefs and drivers to prepare and distribute food during the pandemic in the first weeks of the national lockdown period.Role of Prism in setting up the food projectWhen Aarts realised he needed help setting the project up, he approached Prism through a contact, and the fund said it could help. The arrangement was established within two or three days. Aarts chose to operate as a Collective Fund rather than establish a charity independently. He said the arrangement eased the administrative burden on him and his team, allowing them to focus on running the food project.Prism handled invoices and collected donations, while also advising whether proposed spending was appropriate. This allowed Aarts to concentrate on the work he knew best. The fundraising arrangement also enabled the project to use the government’s Gift Aid scheme, increasing the impact of donations made in the UK.What challenges did the project face as it expandedThe project operated seven days a week and involved coordinating hundreds of volunteers, chefs and drivers. Its first kitchen soon became too small, so the Chair of the Football Association offered Wembley Stadium as a new base. The team continued cooking throughout the move. Although surplus food was central to the operation, donations did not cover every ingredient.The organisers needed to raise money for supplies such as tinned tomatoes and rice. They also had to manage kitchen and delivery rotas, maintain social distancing and follow COVID rules. The project faced logistical and staffing challenges, and Aarts said someone tried to steal money from it.How did the initiative grow into a permanent kitchenAarts said the project was never the work of one person. He described his role as starting the effort and bringing people together, while volunteers and partners made it possible to grow. One organisation he worked closely with was The Felix Project, which provides meals for people in London. The charity wanted a permanent kitchen because demand for the work was expected to continue after COVID. Aarts designed and built the kitchen. About 20 members of his core team moved there, and Felix’s Kitchen opened in July 2021. The kitchen brought together Compassion London and The Felix Project. It continues to prepare 4,500 meals a day using surplus food collected by The Felix Project in London.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Snake in a drain in Basildon gives workers a fright
articles.summary: Water company engineers get "the shock of our lives" after hearing a hissing noise while on a job.
articles.body:
Engineers got "the shock of our lives" when they opened up a drain to find a hissing snake staring back at them.

An Essex and Suffolk Water crew encountered the snake while repairing a leak at Vange in Basildon, Essex.

They stopped work to avoid disturbing the animal and called South Essex Wildlife Hospital to collect it.

"We see all sorts when we're out repairing leaks, but a python was definitely a new one," said a spokesperson for the water company.

The workers came across the snake on Tuesday.

"We'd just set up the site when we started hearing hissing coming from the meter chamber," the spokesperson said.

"We very cautiously lifted it up and got the shock of our lives when we saw a 3-4ft (0.9-1.2m) python staring back at us!"

"No idea how it got in there, but we're pleased that it's now safe and being looked after."

Volunteers from the wildlife hospital at Orsett came to collect it and confirmed it was a non-venomous carpet python, native to Australia and New Guinea, and probably a pet.

Founder Sue Schwar said: "It's just part of the daily jobs that we get thrown at us. We're ready for anything, really."

She said it was possible the snake had escaped, maybe down a toilet, or had been dumped somewhere.

"That does happen quite frequently. So, how it got down under the drain, we've no idea."

She said the snake, which has not been named, was "not very happy" when it was found.

"It was a bit dehydrated and really cold and it's got a few injuries on it, so hopefully we can get it back to health," she said.

"Then, obviously, if an owner doesn't come forward we'll be looking to try and find a home for it."

I wrote an article some months ago saying that this is an unusual situation now, where the Central Government, the Delhi Government, the Haryana Government and the Punjab Government can all be on the same page. None of them is Congress. You don't have to blame us. They can sit together and make a plan,” he said.Tharoor questioned why the Centre and the governments of Delhi and Haryana had not taken concrete steps to tackle the crisis, alleging that the situation was being allowed to spiral out of control.“At least Haryana, Delhi and the Centre, why can't they do something concrete about air pollution? They are allowing this to get completely out of control,” he said.Taking a dig at the pollution levels in the national capital, the Congress leader said it was a relief to breathe Kerala's clean air instead of being in Delhi's polluted atmosphere.“It is a relief to breathe the clean air of Kerala rather than be in the absolutely polluted atmosphere of Delhi,” Tharoor added.GRAP 3 imposed Delhi's air pollution control measures were tightened with the implementation of Stage III of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) on Friday, as the city's air quality deteriorated towards the severe category.The average Air Quality Index (AQI) stood at 382 at 4pm on Friday, up from 369 a day earlier. articles.title: Too Young to Grieve Belfast: The young people helping each other process grief
articles.summary: Too Young to Grieve is an informal peer support community providing young people with a space to grieve.
articles.body:
Luke Alfano was 21 when his dad, who just two weeks earlier had been diagnosed with cancer, died.

At the time, Luke did not know what to do or where to turn.

Five years later, he founded Too Young to Grieve, a community offering young people a casual space to "have a moan, have a laugh, talk about your grief and just know that people understand you".

The group is based in more than 20 locations, including London, Manchester, the US and Australia - and now, Belfast.

Losing someone you love is never easy. But for Luke, the shock of his dad dying so suddenly, and so early in Luke's life, was especially difficult.

"I lost my dad when I was 21. I didn't feel like there was much out there for young adults experiencing loss," Luke told BBC News NI.

"That initial first year or two, I didn't really know what was going on.

"I didn't know what this thing called grief was, I just ignored it."

It was not until Luke, then 25, lost his grandmother that he realised he had "not really processed" his dad's death.

"That experience was a trigger to think back to what happened with my dad and think I don't want to experience that again, so let me try and understand it a bit more," he said.

Luke founded Too Young to Grieve, which offers young people who have experienced grief the opportunity to meet in person, with activities ranging from walks and hikes, to pottery painting and football tournaments.

"When you're 18 to 35, you're grieving someone that most people are going to turn to for a lot of the most important decisions in your life," he said.

"You just want to talk about your person, or just have a space to talk about how you're feeling."

When Chris Guiller's dad died at the age of 57, just five months after being diagnosed with cancer, it came as a shock to the whole family.

"You think you have your parents until later on in life, so when it comes at such a young age, it's difficult," he told BBC News NI.

As a young person, he felt isolated by his grief.

"I didn't have people around me that understood what I was going through," he said.

Almost two years later, Chris now runs the Belfast branch of Too Young to Grieve - an experience he describes as "fantastic".

"You know you're not going through it by yourself. What you're feeling is normal," he added.

In 2025, two days before Christmas, Katherine Macauley's fiancee Peter died following an accident at work.

"I still can't believe that it's real," the 32-year-old said.

Though she believes her grief will "never end", her hope is to find "ways to cope" with it.

And one such way has been Too Young to Grieve.

"Too Young to Grieve is a really lovely way of bringing people together that are in similar situations," she said.

"You feel that you're actually not alone and that other people can have some shared experience with you, and that you can learn from that and you can comfort each other through that.

"It's a really, really wonderful community and group of people."

Luke Alfano said he would like to see resources around grief and coping with bereavement better signposted in schools and universities.

Last year, the Department for Education published statutory guidance that said lessons on loss, grieving and bereavement should take place in primary and secondary schools from September 2026.

However, no such guidance exists in Northern Ireland.

A spokesperson for the Department of Education said "schools have pastoral care policies and structures" so that children know who they can contact if they require support regarding bereavement.

"In terms of curriculum, the Council for the Curriculum, Examinations and Assessment has provided a range of resources which address grief, loss, and bereavement both at primary and post-primary level," they said.

In 2017, William Gregg's mother died. At the time, he did not know "how to handle it".

"It tore me apart for a little while, I sort of lost my way," he said.

"It can be quite catastrophic and emotionally damaging."

William said Too Young to Grieve had been "very helpful".

"It's good to know that there people out there who have gone through something similar and are able to talk about it.

"Whenever I was young, I didn't really have anybody to talk to."

He added that the community has been especially beneficial for his mental health, as the group gives him a space to "express yourself freely".

He said that socialising was especially important for people who were grieving, as they often will not leave the house.

He explained that Too Young to Grieve helped people "build friendships so you have a community around you that you can fall back on".

Chris said the group was "really needed" in Northern Ireland, a region academics have previously said spends less on mental health services per head than other regions, despite having "more complex cases".

"The mental health side of things over here is a bit further behind than other parts of the UK and Ireland," he said.

"You need something like this here because there are a lot of people suffering out there that think they're alone. And they're not.

"I know my dad would be extremely proud."

Luke said the group has helped him grieve.

"Having the opportunity to share things about my dad has given me a great perspective on grief, and it's helped me on my own healing journey as well," he said.

So what does Luke think his dad would make of the group built in his legacy?

"My dad wanted me to be a professional footballer. Unfortunately I wasn't quite good enough.

"But in terms of the community we've built, it could fill a lot of professional stadiums."

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Postgraduate doctors are walking away from residency programmes at some of India's leading medical institutions.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Postgraduate doctors are walking away from residency programmes at some of India's leading medical institutions. RTI replies show exits across AIIMS campuses and JIPMER, with AIIMS Delhi alone reporting 34 junior resident departures in 2025.While several institutes lack consolidated data on psychiatric counselling or workplace stress among residents, Dr Lakshya Mittal, chairperson of United Doctors Front (UDF), said multiple RTI applications filed by its members had revealed postgraduate doctors quitting premier medical institutions despite securing top NEET-PG ranks. He cited complaints of duties extending beyond 36 hours, workplace harassment, toxic work culture and inadequate support.“Residency is meant to train doctors, not break them. Discipline is not humiliation and dedication is not exploitation,” Mittal said, urging authorities to enforce working-hour regulations, establish independent grievance-redressal mechanisms and fix institutional accountability. UDF has also filed a PIL in the Supreme Court.However, the figures from individual institutions show that departures have continued, even as some reported a decline. At AIIMS Delhi, 34 junior resident doctors quit in 2025, compared with 60 in 2024, a decline of about 43%. The number of residents joining also fell, from 324 in 2024 to 267 in 2025. Department-wise figures show the highest number of exits in anaesthesiology at seven, followed by ophthalmology at six. Surgery reported three exits, as did pathology. Ophthalmology had recorded 14 exits in 2024.JIPMER, Puducherry, also reported a decline in resignations. A combined count of departures from its January and July batches shows 44 residents resigned in 2025, compared with 60 in 2024, a fall of nearly 27%. However, exits continued across several specialities, including anaesthesiology, emergency medicine, orthopaedics, pathology and surgery.The trend is not confined to these two institutions. AIIMS Kalyani reported 15 exits across all three years of postgraduate training in 2025, including 13 from the January and July batches. Another 11 students from the 2026 batches had left by the time of its reply. AIIMS Raipur reported 19 exits from its 2025 batches, AIIMS Patna 12, while AIIMS Gorakhpur also reported departures. At AIIMS Rishikesh, 30 students across various postgraduate and super-speciality programmes left in 2025.The RTI also sought details of psychiatric counselling and whether stress, depression or sleep deprivation were recorded as reasons for leaving. AIIMS Delhi said it had no compiled counselling data, while AIIMS Rishikesh reported six postgraduate students receiving psychiatric counselling in 2026 but maintained no consolidated record of workplace-related stress. AIIMS Raipur reported no residents seeking counselling in 2025 or 2026. AIIMS Patna reported 15 residents receiving counselling in 2025 and none in 2026, while AIIMS Kalyani declined to provide the information, citing RTI provisions.The figures are not directly comparable as institutes provided data for different periods and batches. articles.body: Bill Gates ex-wife and philanthropist Melinda Gates has offered followers a glimpse inside her office, showcasing three personal items that she says bring her joy while also reinforcing her long-standing advocacy for women’s advancement and leadership. In a video shared on social media platform Instagram, the Gates showed the viewers what she described as tour of “a few things that bring me JOY in my office.” The video shared featured various items such as a figurine of late US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, a vintage board game titled “The Exciting Game of Career Girls,” and a piece of artwork displaying the word “JOY.” As per an Inc. report, the video has been viewed by more than 1.2 million people.Ginsburg quote remains a source of inspirationAmong the items, French Gates highlighted a figurine gifted by her younger brother that honours Ginsburg, whom she described as a major influence. She used the item to draw attention to one of the late justice's most widely cited observations: “Women belong in all places where decisions are made.” According to the report, French Gates also displayed a framed version of the quote signed by Ginsburg.The message aligns closely with French Gates' philanthropic work, which has focused heavily on improving opportunities for women and families. Through Pivotal, the organisation she founded in 2015, she has directed significant investments toward women's health and gender equality initiatives. Earlier this year, she pledged an additional $215 million to the organisation, bringing her total commitment over the previous two years to $600 million to support areas including contraception and maternal healthcare, according to Pivotal.A reminder of progress for womenAnother item featured in the office tour was “The Exciting Game of Career Girls,” a board game from the 1950s. The game, which depicts careers such as nurse, stewardess and teacher as desirable options for women, serves as a reminder of how opportunities have expanded over time, French Gates said. “It reminds me that we actually have made a lot of progress when you think about all the different types of careers women have these days,” she said, according to the report. The comments expand on a theme that has long shaped her public advocacy: increasing women's participation in leadership roles and decision-making positions across society.The artwork behind her deskThe final item in the office tour was a large artwork reading “JOY,” which hangs above her desk. According to French Gates, the letters are composed of numerous small human figures, symbolising the idea of shared happiness and community. “Each little blob represents a different person, and it's a representation of collective joy,” she said. “If we have joy in our lives, if we share it with somebody else, it doubles that joy.” She added that the artwork frequently draws comments from people during video calls, with many noticing the word displayed behind her and responding positively to it.Focus on women’s healthFrench Gates’s philanthropy centres on advancing women and families. In 2015 she founded Pivotal, an organisation focused on women’s health. Earlier this year she pledged an additional $215 million to it, bringing her total commitment over the past two years to $600 million, according to Pivotal’s website. articles.title: Paper lanterns and Akash Kandil: How to make your own in 30 minutes
articles.summary: Creating your own Diwali decorations, such as colorful paper lanterns and Akash Kandil, can turn into an enjoyable family project.
articles.body: Creating your own Diwali decorations, such as colorful paper lanterns and Akash Kandil, can turn into an enjoyable family project. Utilizing basic materials like colored paper, glue, and scissors allows everyone to participate. These handcrafted items not only add a special charm to your celebrations but also promote eco-friendliness. Involving children in the crafting process brings an extra dose of happiness to the festivities and strengthens family bonds. Prepare to illuminate your Diwali with a splash of color and eco-friendliness by making your own paper lanterns and Akash Kandil. Gather evryone for this joyous crafting experience, utilizing simple supplies to add a personal flair to your home this Diwali.Paper lanternPaper lanterns are quite delicate, and the light that comes through them is soft and warm. To make them, all you need is a pencil, coloured paper, an eraser, glue and a pen-style paper knife.Firstly, fold two A4-size sheets of cardstock in half and then stick them together to form a cuboid. The third sheet of cardstock needs to be cut into square shapes to cover the top and bottom of this cuboid. This is the basic layout, and based on the changes in dimensions and the designs you make on the side panels, you get a different paper lantern each time.Open up the A4-size cardstock sheets that you had folded and draw the cut-out designs on the panels with a pencil. Stick a piece of tissue paper behind each cut-out. Fold and stick the four panels together to make a tall box with a square base. Cut two squares from separate sheets of cardstock and stick one on each side. Stick the bottom one with tape like a flap so you can open it to slip the light inside and finally make a paper lantern.You can vary the lantern design by changing the cut-out patterns. Instead of cutting out a plain big rectangle, cut out patterns or designs, and I am sure you will not stop making these lanterns. You can vary the pattern and create different lanterns of your choice.Making an Akash KandilAn Akash Kandil, which may also be spelled as Akash Kandeel, is a vibrant and traditional decorative lantern that is elegantly hung outside homes during the auspicious Hindu festival of Diwali. This ritual is particularly significant in the state of Maharashtra and is widely celebrated across various regions of India. The Akash Kandil holds a special place in the Diwali festivities in Maharashtra, as this custom has been integrated into family and community celebrations for many generations. While other regions in India partake in illuminating diyas (traditional earthen lamps) and setting off fireworks, Maharashtra has embraced the sky lantern as a distinctive hallmark of the festival. In both urban areas and rural villages, families come together on rooftops and in open spaces to collectively release these beautiful lanterns into the night sky, resulting in a breathtaking spectacle of numerous lights ascending into the dark.To make the Akash Kandil, you need some tissue paper or butter paper, preferably butter paper because it will allow the light to glow through and is stronger than tissue paper.Now, let's see how you can make a large five-pointed star on a thin card, about 25-39 cm wide. On each of them, cut a few windows or small shapes, then stick tissue paper behind them in different colours. Cut five strips of card, four centimetres wide, and fold a small tab at both ends.This year, rather than heading directly to the market to buy decorations, take a moment to grab a pair of scissors along with some vibrant coloured sheets. Engage in the creative process of making your very own DIY Diwali decorations. By opting for this thoughtful approach, you can significantly reduce your consumption and minimize waste by avoiding any unnecessary purchases that typically accompany the festive season.Here's an additional tip to consider: If you’re feeling particularly creative and would like to try something special, think about skipping the use of basic shapes or perhaps incorporating a delightful strip of gold or silver paper along the edges. Furthermore, you could enhance your Akash Kandil or paper lanterns by gluing tiny, charming paper flowers to them. For the Akash Kandil specifically, why not tie a fancy tassel or a few colorful strands of thread to each point of the star? This will create a lovely effect as they sway gently in the breeze. Additionally, a string of small beads or even a marigold garland could be added to embellish the bottom of the decoration. Don’t stop at just making one; encourage your children to join in the festive spirit! Together, you can create multiple decorations to beautifully adorn various parts of your home.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. articles.title: CM Devendra Fadnavis to spend Diwali Night with farmers in Narkhed village
articles.summary: Nagpur: Chief minister Devendra Fadnavis will celebrate Diwali with drought-hit farmers at Lohari Sawanga village in Narkhed taluka of Nagpur district on
articles.body: Nagpur: Chief minister Devendra Fadnavis will celebrate Diwali with drought-hit farmers at Lohari Sawanga village in Narkhed taluka of Nagpur district on Saturday, in an effort to boost the morale of the farming community grappling with an agrarian crisis.Fadnavis will leave Nagpur on Saturday evening and spend the night in the village, interacting with farmers and their families. He is expected to discuss issues concerning agriculture, including irrigation facilities, crop insurance, water availability and other local problems.The visit assumes significance in the backdrop of the severe drought-like situation in the state, which has affected agricultural activities and pushed several farming families into financial distress. Through the initiative, Fadnavis intends to convey that the government stands firmly with farmers during difficult times and that they are not alone in facing the crisis.On Sunday morning, the chief minister is scheduled to hold a meeting with elected representatives from Narkhed taluka to discuss local issues. During his return journey, he is also likely to stop at a few villages to inspect agricultural fields and review ongoing water conservation works.Fadnavis had earlier appealed to all ministers in the state cabinet to spend at least one day during Diwali with farmers in a village. He said the initiative would help ministers understand the difficulties faced by farming families, share their joys and sorrows and provide them emotional support.He had also emphasised that farmers' distress affects not just agricultural households but the entire rural economy, and called for collective efforts by the government, people's representatives, social organisations and citizens to extend relief.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Nagpur | Silver Rate in Nagpur | Bank Holidays in Nagpur | Public Holidays in Nagpur | Petrol Price in Nagpur | Diesel Price in Nagpur | CNG Price in Nagpur | LPG Price in NagpurStay updated with the latest Nagpur news. articles.title: 'Then in Ghaziabad, now Illinois': Saba Haider on how upbringing shaped her values after midterm win
articles.summary: Indian-origin Democrat Saba Haider, who became the first South Asian woman to be elected to the Illinois General Assembly, has credited her upbringing in
articles.body: Indian-origin Democrat Saba Haider, who became the first South Asian woman to be elected to the Illinois General Assembly, has credited her upbringing in Ghaziabad and her parents' approach to helping others for shaping her commitment to public service.Haider won the November 3 US midterm election from Illinois' 84th House District, securing 20,756 votes, or 70.9 per cent, against Republican candidate Brian Scopa.In a statement shared with the media by her family in Ghaziabad, Haider said the values she learnt at home continued to guide her even after moving to the US around 20 years ago. "In our house, we never asked how much money you have, or where you are from. We only asked: What do you need? Then in Ghaziabad, now in Illinois, the same family, same rule," she said, as quoted by PTI.Haider recalled that her parents regularly helped people in their neighbourhood, irrespective of their background. Her father, a government engineer, and her mother, who managed the household, would help neighbours with hospital visits, provide books to children, assist elderly residents and support families moving into the locality.She said she began following the same approach as a teenager by tutoring younger children for free, checking on elderly neighbours and helping organise community activities. "My father taught me that privilege is not for comfort; it is for service. He built public infrastructure with honesty all day, and came home to serve his own neighbourhood," Haider said.She added that her parents' influence had shaped her focus on issues such as the cost of living, affordable education and safer communities for children. "For my family, helping someone in need was never politics. It was just how we lived," she said.Haider, 42 has her family roots to Aurangabad in Uttar Pradesh's Bulandshahr district. She said her journey into electoral politics in the US involved extensive campaigning, including door-to-door outreach across Chicago suburbs during the winter primary season.In an interview with PTI Videos, she said voters were increasingly focusing on everyday concerns such as affordability, healthcare, education and the environment. "If the candidates are talking about those issues, like everyday kitchen table issues, people are paying attention to that," she said, adding that voters were responding to candidates addressing problems affecting families and their children.Haider also spoke about the scrutiny women face in electoral politics, saying they are judged on everything from the colour of their lipstick to the length of their sleeves.She urged young South Asian Americans interested in public service to get involved in local election campaigns and build support across communities.You use AI every day.
